SK2193 ImmutableArray<T> is built with a collection initializer

new ImmutableArray<T> { … } calls Add on the default value of the struct, which wraps a null array, so the first element throws NullReferenceException.

CategoryCorrectness
Default severityerror
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, review it
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

The collection-initializer form is sugar for Add calls on whatever new produced, and for this type new produces default — a struct around a null reference. The line reads like list construction, compiles without a word, and throws on the first element every single time it runs. It is a trap on one type specifically, which is what makes it survive being read.

Example

Instead of:

var ids = new System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray<int> { 1, 2, 3 };

Write:

var ids = System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray.Create<int>(1, 2, 3);

When it does not fire

⚠ Measured, not assumed: the shape builds clean. A probe outside this repository compiles it with no compiler warning and nothing from the .NET analyzers at AnalysisMode=All, so nothing in the toolchain says a word before it runs. ⚠ An empty initializer is excluded and is a different, weaker defect. new ImmutableArray<T> { } calls Add zero times and therefore does not throw; it silently yields a default array whose IsDefault is true, which fails later and somewhere else. Reporting it under this rule's message — which says the code throws — would be saying something untrue about it. ⚠ The parser is what excludes it, and the element-count check is not — a sabotage run found that out. An empty brace pair is ambiguous between the two initializer forms and Roslyn classifies it ObjectInitializerExpression, so a CollectionInitializerExpression with zero expressions does not exist and relaxing the count changes nothing. The count stays as a statement of intent that would survive a parser change; it is not what does the work today. An element that is itself a braced group is excluded too, because a multi-argument Add does not exist on this type. ⚠ The fix reuses the type's own spelling rather than assuming an import. ImmutableArray<int> becomes ImmutableArray.Create<int>(…) and System.Collections.Immutable.ImmutableArray<int> keeps its qualifier, so the replacement binds in exactly the files the original bound in. The type argument is written out explicitly because inference from the elements is not the same answer: new ImmutableArray<object> { 1 } is an array of object and ImmutableArray.Create(1) is an array of int. ⚠ The collection-expression spelling `[…]` is deliberately not the fix, even though C# 12 makes it correct on this type: it needs a target type, and var ids = new ImmutableArray<int> { 1 }; has none, so a fix that used it would be right in most places and produce CS9176 in the rest. The target-typed new() { … } spelling has no type syntax to reuse and is not reported. A span carrying a comment or a preprocessor directive is not rewritten. fixIsSafe: false: the edit turns code that throws into code that runs, which is a behaviour change even though it is the intended one.
